content.title: About
content.content: Upma is a traditional South Indian dish made from semolina (suji) that is steamed with spices, vegetables, and sometimes legumes. The dish has a soft, slightly fluffy texture and is flavored with aromatic herbs such as mustard seeds, curry leaves, and turmeric.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Upma is commonly eaten for breakfast, but it can be enjoyed at any time of day.
There are many regional variations: Kerala adds coconut milk, Andhra Pradesh includes lentils, and Tamil Nadu incorporates nuts and dried fruits.
The dish is considered light and easily digestible, making it a frequent choice for the sick and for children.
Traditionally upma is cooked in a special steam pot (uruli), but it can also be prepared in a regular skillet.
The semolina used in upma is rich in carbohydrates and provides a quick source of energy.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Semolina releases glucose slowly, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Upma contains thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Because it uses modest amounts of oil, the dish fits well into low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Added vegetables and legumes increase fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Turmeric and mustard seeds have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Semolina is made from wheat, so people with celiac disease should use gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Large portions of upma can raise blood sugar quickly.

items.title: Salt and oil content
items.content: Recipes often call for generous amounts of oil and salt, which may be unsuitable for hypertension.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Some versions include hot chilies that can irritate the stomach of sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot upma with chutney, yogurt, or coconut sauce. Garnish with toasted nuts, fresh herbs, and a squeeze of lime for extra flavor. A “plain” version can be made without oil, using vegetable broth instead.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked upma in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in a skillet with a splash of water or oil to restore its soft texture.
